title: Build a cold outreach personalization engine
description: A system that drafts a personalized cold email for one prospect using a real signal about them, and refuses to draft without one.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

merge.title: Merge
merge.content: Combining changes from one branch into another. When you approve a pull request, the branch gets merged into main and those changes become part of the live version.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

hubspot.title: HubSpot
hubspot.content: A CRM and marketing platform used by sales, marketing, and customer success teams. Common target for AI automations — students connect it to draft outreach, enrich contacts, or sync data with other tools.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

authentication.title: Authentication
authentication.content: The process of proving your identity so Claude can access a tool or service on your behalf. Usually happens through OAuth (a login popup) or an API key.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Most cold email reads like a mail-[merge](#tooltip-merge) with a name dropped in, and prospects treat it that way. Signal-based personalized campaigns average an 18 percent reply rate, more than five times the roughly 3.4 percent average for generic templated cold email, per [Autobound's Cold Email Guide](https://www.autobound.ai/blog/cold-email-guide-2026). This system takes one target account and one real signal, such as a funding round, a job posting, or a product launch, and drafts an opening line built around it.

Copy quality only matters if the email lands. Google requires senders of 5,000 or more daily messages to have SPF, DKIM, and DMARC aligned, enforced since November 2025, per [Google Workspace's sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/14229414). A domain with weak [authentication](#tooltip-authentication) gets throttled no matter how sharp the personalization is.

Run it as a paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt) before each send, a saved skill in your sequencing [workflow](#tooltip-workflow), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that drafts against a signal feed. Every version still leaves the send to a person.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming where your signals will come from, your offer and audience, and what personalized sounds like coming from you.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that drafts personalized cold outreach based on a real signal about each prospect, not a template with a name dropped in. Ask me questions, one at a time, about where I'll get signals, my offer and audience, and what personalized sounds like from me. Then write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview forces you to define what counts as a real signal before you draft a single email, and that definition becomes the filter for every draft after it.

items: Where your prospecting signals will come from.
Your current sending volume and domain authentication status.
How much personalization is worth spending per prospect.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common [connectors](#tooltip-tool-connectors) are enrichment data (Apollo, Clay), your sequencing tool (Outreach, Salesloft, Instantly), and your CRM (Salesforce, [HubSpot](#tooltip-hubspot)). The paste-in version needs none.

**Create.** Start building the system your scope document describes, and test it on a real, dated signal you have in hand. The prompt below is an example of the core task. Your scope document will give you a version shaped to your setup.

children.prompt:
Goal: Draft a short cold email to [contact] at [company] using [signal] as the hook.

Context: My offer is [one sentence]; length is [X words]; the signal is [describe it and its source].

Rules:
- No draft without a real, dated signal.
- Never invent a company fact.
- One clear ask.
- Under [X] words.
- Flag signals older than [30/60] days.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: requiring a dated signal before any draft keeps the system from falling back on a generic template the moment a good signal isn't handy.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Real signal named, no invented facts, one ask, under your word limit?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what missed ("too salesy in the close, cut the last line") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Add a suppression check before send.
Report which signal types get replies.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat turn the scope bar into pass/fail checks and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each cold email draft, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, signal type, whether it was sent or held, reply received, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call on what counts as personalized, and the log surfaces which signal types earn a reply after a few weeks of entries.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Each entry takes a minute. Note the date, which rubric checks passed or failed, and what you changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the system passes the rubric a couple weeks straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill. A check that fails again and again is a candidate for a skill of its own. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write the skill for you, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).
One durable failure mode. Unreviewed AI outreach at scale is the most common way this backfires, and it can damage a domain's reputation in the process.
